questions.q: Why does classical physics predict that almost no cosmic muons should reach sea level?
options: Muons are created too close to the ground to gather enough speed
A muon lives only about 2.2 microseconds, so even at light speed it can travel at most about 660 m before decaying — far short of the 15 km journey
The atmosphere absorbs all muons within the first kilometre
Muons are repelled by the Earth's magnetic field before they can land
questions.explanation: Using distance = speed x time with the proper lifetime of 2.2 microseconds, even a muon at the full speed of light covers only about 660 m. Since the muons are born about 15 km up, classical physics says they should die more than 14 km short of the ground.

questions.q: What does the term 'proper lifetime' of the muon refer to?
options: The lifetime measured by an observer on the ground watching the muon fly past
The 2.2 microsecond average lifetime measured in the muon's own rest frame, where its birth and decay happen at the same place
The longest possible lifetime any muon could ever have
The half-life of a population of muons, about 1.5 microseconds
questions.explanation: The proper lifetime is the time measured in the muon's own rest frame — the frame in which birth and decay occur at the same place. It is the fixed value (about 2.2 microseconds) that never changes, no matter how the muon moves relative to anyone else.

questions.q: Which two postulates form the basis of Einstein's special theory of relativity (1905)?
options: Mass increases with speed; energy equals mass times c squared
The laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame; the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for every observer regardless of motion
Time is absolute for all observers; space is curved by mass
Light always travels in straight lines; gravity bends time
questions.explanation: Special relativity rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are identical in every inertial (constant-velocity) frame, and light in a vacuum travels at the same speed for every observer. The second postulate is the one that forces time itself to give.

questions.q: What happens to the Lorentz factor (gamma) as a particle's speed v approaches the speed of light c?
options: Gamma stays close to 1, so time dilation is always negligible
Gamma shrinks toward zero, so the clock speeds up
Gamma blows up toward infinity, so the moving clock runs more and more slowly relative to a stationary observer
Gamma equals exactly v divided by c
questions.explanation: Gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2). When v is small, gamma is about 1 and dilation is negligible; but as v approaches c the quantity under the root shrinks toward zero and gamma blows up. At 98% of c gamma is about 5; at 99.97% it is around 40.

questions.q: How does the muon's survival look different when viewed from the muon's own frame rather than the Earth's frame?
options: From the muon's frame nothing reaches the ground; only the Earth frame explains survival
From the Earth frame the muon's clock runs slow (time dilation); from the muon's frame the atmosphere is squashed thin (length contraction) — both give the same outcome
From the muon's frame its lifetime stretches to 33 microseconds, just as it does from Earth
From the muon's frame the muon speeds up to exactly the speed of light
questions.explanation: In the Earth frame, time dilation slows the muon's decay clock so it lives long enough to cross the full 15 km. In the muon's own frame, the clock ticks normally but length contraction squashes the 15 km of atmosphere down to about 1 km. The two frames disagree about why, but agree the muon reaches the ground.

questions.q: How did the Frisch and Smith Mount Washington experiment (1962-63) confirm time dilation?
options: They predicted 27 muons per hour at sea level classically but 409 actually survived, matching Einstein's relativistic prediction of about 400
They found exactly 27 muons per hour at the bottom, confirming the classical prediction
They measured the muon's mass and showed it increased with speed
They proved muons travel faster than light down the mountain
questions.explanation: Counting about 565 muons per hour at the summit, the classical (no time dilation) prediction was only about 27 per hour surviving to Cambridge, while relativity predicted around 400. They measured 409 plus or minus 9 per hour — almost exactly Einstein's number and nowhere near Newton's.

questions.q: Why must GPS satellites have relativity built into them to function correctly?
options: Their radio signals travel slower than light through the atmosphere

Combining special relativity (motion slows the clock) and general relativity (weaker gravity speeds it up), satellite clocks run fast by about 38 microseconds per day, which would drift positions by about 10 km per day if uncorrected
The satellites move so slowly that relativity makes their clocks run slow by 38 microseconds per day
Relativity changes the satellites' orbit but not their clocks
questions.explanation: Special relativity (orbital speed) slows the satellite clocks by about 7.2 microseconds per day, while general relativity (weaker gravity at altitude) speeds them up by about 45.8 microseconds per day, for a net gain of about 38 microseconds per day. Uncorrected, that error would push position fixes off by roughly 10 km each day, so engineers pre-tune the clocks before launch.

questions.q: From memory: explain the two-frame resolution of the muon puzzle — what each frame says about why the muon reaches the ground.
keyPoints: Earth frame: the muon moves fast, so its decay clock runs slow (time dilation), and its lifetime stretches by gamma — long enough to cross the full 15 km.
Muon frame: the muon's clock ticks normally and it lives only its proper 2.2 microseconds, but the 15 km of atmosphere is length-contracted by gamma down to about 1 km, which it can cross in time.
Both frames disagree about the mechanism but agree on the outcome — the muon arrives — and that self-consistency is the signature that relativity is correct.
questions.explanation: If you recalled time dilation for the Earth frame, length contraction for the muon frame, and that both give the same result, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: describe the Hafele-Keating experiment (1971) and what it demonstrated.
keyPoints: Four caesium atomic clocks were flown around the world eastward then westward on commercial jets, each booked its own seat under the name 'Mister Clock', while identical reference clocks stayed at the Naval Observatory.

Two effects competed: special relativity (motion slows the flying clocks) and general relativity (weaker gravity at altitude speeds them up), and Earth's rotation made the east and west flights differ.

Eastbound clocks lost 59 ns (predicted about 40) and westbound gained 273 ns (predicted 275), confirming relativity — the twin paradox made real with clocks that genuinely read different times on landing.
questions.explanation: If you recalled the flying-clocks setup, the two competing relativistic effects, and that the clocks disagreed on landing as predicted, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: A muon at rest lives for a proper lifetime of 2.2 microseconds. Travelling at nearly the speed of light, how far could it travel before decaying according to classical physics? Assume v = c = 3 x 10^8 m/s.
questions.explanation: Classical distance = speed x time gives only about 660 m even at the full speed of light — far short of the 15 km journey, which is why classical physics says almost no muons should reach the ground.

questions.q: For a muon with a Lorentz factor of gamma = 15, find the dilated lifetime measured in the Earth frame, given a proper lifetime of 2.2 microseconds.
questions.explanation: The dilated time in our frame is gamma times the proper lifetime: 15 x 2.2 = 33 microseconds. With this much time at nearly light speed the muon can cover about 10 km, comfortably reaching the ground.
